title: Cullen Skink
subtitle: Scottish smoked haddock, potato, and leek chowder
excerpt: Cullen skink is a thick, creamy Scottish soup from the town of Cullen in Aberdeenshire: smoked haddock, potato, and onion or leek in a milk-and-cream broth. It is made without stock , the milk absorbs the flavour of the fish as it poaches. The result is deeply smoky, naturally salty, and very warming.
sourceNotes: Cullen skink takes its name from Cullen, a fishing village on the Moray Firth in north-east Scotland. The word skink is an old Scottish term for a soup or essence, related to the shin of beef. The recipe is entirely built around the Finnan haddock that was smoked in the region.

recipe.batchNotes: Make up to 2 days ahead. Reheat gently to avoid the milk splitting.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 days ahead. Reheat gently without boiling.

content.text: Cullen skink uses milk as its base, not stock. The smoked haddock poaches in the milk and flavours it completely. Use the best undyed smoked haddock you can find: the artificial yellow dye adds colour but detracts from flavour. The soup should be creamy and thick but not gluey; the potato gives it body but should not turn it into a pure.

Put the smoked haddock in a wide pan, skin side down. Pour over {{whole-milk}} of milk. Add the bay leaf. Bring to a gentle simmer and poach for 8 minutes until the fish flakes easily. Lift out the fish, remove the skin and any bones, and flake the flesh. Reserve the milk.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a large pan over medium heat. Cook {{onion}} chopped onion and {{leek}} sliced leek for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{potato}} diced potato and pour over the reserved poaching milk. Simmer for 15 minutes until the potato is tender.

Remove about one-third of the potato with a slotted spoon and mash roughly. Return to the soup to thicken it. Stir in {{double-cream}} of double cream. Season carefully with pepper and taste before adding salt: the fish has already salted the milk. Fold in the flaked haddock. Serve in warm bowls with chopped parsley on top.

items.cause: Smoked haddock releases salt into the milk during poaching.
items.fix: Do not add salt until the very end, and only after tasting. The poaching milk will carry all the salt the soup needs.

items.symptom: The milk has split and curdled
items.cause: The soup was brought to a boil rather than kept at a gentle simmer.
items.fix: Keep the soup below a boil at all times. Reheat gently; a high heat will cause the milk to split.

items.symptom: The soup is thin and watery
items.cause: Insufficient potato, or the potato was not partially mashed to thicken the soup.
items.fix: Mash one-third of the potato back into the soup. This is the traditional thickening method , no flour or cream thickener is needed.

items.cause: The fish was removed from the milk too quickly, or the milk was not fully reduced.
items.fix: The full 8-minute poach is needed to transfer flavour to the milk. Taste the poaching milk before using it in the soup , it should taste of fish, not just cream.

content.text: Cullen skink is the most celebrated soup of Scottish cooking. It appears on the menu of almost every hotel and restaurant in the Highlands and the north-east. It is often cited as a model of what Scottish regional cooking does well: building a lot of flavour from very few ingredients. Finnan haddock, the cold-smoked undyed variety from the town of Finnan near Aberdeen, is the traditional choice. Any good undyed smoked haddock is a fair substitute.
